Where he struck, the earth split and valleys formed. Where he stepped, passes opened through ranges that had no name. The Wakhan Corridor, the elders say, was made by his left foot. The Bartang Valley was the scrape of his staff as he paused to rest. And the great plateau of the Pamir, flat and high as a table set for gods, was where he sat to catch his breath.

But the Farsakh Walker grew weary. The distance between suns is longer than any mortal can imagine, and even giants feel the weight of such a task. Near the end of his journey, his steps shortened. The valleys became narrower, the passes more steep and treacherous. This, the people say, is why the eastern passes are so much harder than the western ones.

When at last he completed his measurement, the sky master counted the farsakh marks and found the answer: one hundred thousand farsakhs between dawn and dusk. 'It is enough,' the sky master declared, and the day was fixed at its proper length. The Farsakh Walker was rewarded with sleep. He lay down in the high Pamir, and his body became the range of mountains that the people now call the Giants' Spine.

Shepherds still find enormous stones in the high passes, smooth and round, which they say are the Farsakh Walker's footprints filled with centuries of snow. And on still nights, some claim they can hear the echo of his iron staff striking the earth, measuring out the world for those who still walk between the wells.
themes: the shaping of landscape by mythic forces
weariness and mortality of even great beings
moral: Even the greatest among us are shaped by the tasks they carry, and the marks they leave upon the world endure long after they rest.
source: Tajik oral tradition, Persian/Central Asian folklore

title: The Fire Keeper of the Gaucho Camps
summary: A spirit of the campfire who appears to gauchos in the wilderness, testing their hospitality and generosity.
full_text:
There is a story the old gauchos tell around the fire, when the embers glow low and the chimarrão gourd passes from hand to hand. They speak of the Fire Keeper, a spirit who tends the flame of every campfire in the Uruguayan wilderness. He appears as a wizened old man with ash-gray skin and eyes that glow like burning coals. He carries no weapon, only a long iron rod for stirring the fire.

The Fire Keeper does not punish the wicked or reward the virtuous in any grand way. His test is smaller and more intimate. When a gaucho makes camp alone on the pampas, the Fire Keeper may approach in the guise of a weary traveler. He will ask for shelter by the fire, for a sip of mate, for a piece of the roasted meat. If the gaucho shares freely and without complaint, the Fire Keeper stirs the embers and vanishes. The gaucho's fire will burn bright all night, never needing more wood, and his dreams will show him where the cattle have wandered. But if the gaucho refuses, if he clutches his food and his warmth to himself, the Fire Keeper will let the fire die. The gaucho will spend the night in darkness and cold, and in the morning he will find his horse gone and his way lost.

A young gaucho named Facundo once refused the Fire Keeper, thinking him a beggar unworthy of his hospitality. He woke to find his fire cold, his horse vanished, and the pampas stretching in every direction without a landmark. He walked for three days before the Fire Keeper appeared again. Facundo fell to his knees and offered everything he had. The Fire Keeper smiled, lit a new fire with a touch of his finger, and said, 'Now you understand.' Facundo never forgot that lesson. He became known as the most generous man on the pampas, and his fires never went cold again.
moral: Generosity to strangers brings its own warmth.

title: Falcone, the Sammarinese Winged Guardian
summary: A monstrous winged creature said to inhabit Mount Titano, Falcone is a guardian of San Marino who protects the republic from invasion.
full_text:
San Marino, the oldest republic in the world, sits atop Mount Titano. According to legend, when Saint Marinus founded his community of refugees on the mountain in the 4th century, he was not alone. A great winged creature, Falcone, watched over him from the cliffs. Falcone was a monster in appearance but not in spirit: he had the body of a lion, the wings of an eagle, and a voice like rolling thunder. Saint Marinus, with his gentle faith, did not fear the beast. He blessed it, and Falcone became the protector of the new republic.

Over the centuries, Falcone has defended San Marino many times. When armies marched against the tiny republic, Falcone would appear on the cliffs, spreading his immense wings and roaring with a sound that echoed across the valleys. Invading soldiers, seeing the monstrous shape against the sky, would flee in terror. The Sammarinese people learned to trust their winged guardian.

But Falcone is not always visible. He sleeps in a cave beneath the Guaita fortress, awakening only when the republic is in danger. In times of peace, he cannot be seen at all, only occasionally heard, a distant rumble from the mountain's heart. The people of San Marino still tell their children about Falcone, the winged beast who chose to serve a saint rather than terrorize the land. He is a reminder that even monsters can be guardians and that the smallest nation on earth has the fiercest protector.
moral: True strength serves the weak, not preys upon them.
